To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the right hemisphere is crucial for face processing; the OFA and FFA are the core regions of this process, but they are not the only regions that respond to faces; the OFA is a necessary but not sufficient region for face processing; and that the FFA is a necessary and sufficient region for face recognition.

the right OFA, the right FFA and the right STS/TPJ are all necessary for the perception of faces, that these three regions are all involved in the processing of other categories of visual objects, but that their relative contributions to the processing of these other categories of objects are different.
the right hemisphere is crucial for face processing and that the right ‘OFA’ plays a key role in the elaboration of individual face percepts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the cortical networks involved in face perception, in particular in the human brain (see Sergent, 2006 for a review).
the neural basis of face recognition in humans, with particular emphasis on the role of the right fusiform face area (FFA).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“the face is processed in the cortex”.
the cortical face network includes the core regions of Alumit Ishais’ model and that these regions are part of a wider cortical network.
the cortical face network is a large network, which includes at least the core areas of the right fusiform gyrus and the occipital face areas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the face is a “complex visual pattern” and the face processing system is a “complex perceptual system”.
we have been able to show that the right hemisphere, more specifically its posterior region, plays a crucial role in the processing of individual faces.
face processing in the human brain involves the interaction between two major systems, one specialized to process faces and the other specialized for object perception.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the right hemisphere is necessary to elaborate a full individual face perception.
the cortical face network is distributed and involves multiple cortical and subcortical regions.
face processing is a complex, distributed process that is not restricted to the fusiform face area.
